source_title: Greek shipwreck's 2,000-year-old device was built to predict eclipses
source_excerpt: "Astronomy compels the soul to look upwards and leads us from this world to another" said Plato. But even as the skies above us have changed over centuries, the stars have continued to hold the same fascination for those seeking to understand the universe. There are some discoveries that do not immediately reveal to us the extent of what they hold within them, lying quietly beneath layers of dust and corrosion until someone curious enough comes along and happens to look a little closer.The discovery of the Antikythera Mechanism is one such story where a seemingly unostentatious piece of corroded bronze was recovered from the depths of the Mediterranean, revealing an extraordinary knowledge of astronomy and mechanical engineering that had existed more than 2,000 years ago.What appeared to be a little more than a lump of metal was, in fact, later revealed to be an elaborate astronomical calculator, built by the ancient greeks to follow the movements of celestial bodies and predict events in the skies.It was in 1990, when a group of Greek sponge divers discovered an ancient shipwreck off the coast of Antikythera, an island situated between Crete and Peloponnese. The divers who were exploring the seabed came across the remains of a large cargo vessel,whre pottery, glassware, statues and other antique objects lay scattered. Looking at this, recovery operations followed from 1901 to well into 1920, with several artefacts eventually being brought to the National Archaeolgical Museum in Athens.An unexpected discoveryAmong these copious objects gathered, there was also a heavily corroded mass of bronze, which at first gathered very little interest of researchers. However, it was only in 1902, that when archaeolgists examined the object more closely, that this small toothed gear became prominent.The object came to be known as the Antikythera Mechanism, named after the island near which it was discovered. Although its original appearance has been obscured by centuries underwater, researchers have been able to reconstruct much of its internal arrangement through modern imaging technologies.In a 2006 study published in Nature, researchers, including Tony Freeth and his colleagues, used high-resolution X-ray tomography and surface imaging to examine the surviving fragments, revealing a sophisticated arrangement of interlocking bronze gears. The study established that the mechanism was capable of calculating astronomical cycles, including the movements of the Sun and Moon, while also predicting solar and lunar eclipses.Why was the gear used 2,000 years agoWhat makes the discovery particularly remarkable is the complexity hidden within its construction. The mechanism contained at least 30 bronze gear wheels, arranged in a system that allowed the movement of one component to correspond with the changing positions of celestial bodies. Rather than simply marking the passage of days or months, it could represent the relationship between different astronomical cycles.Apart from its astronomical calculations, the mechanism also carried a connection to the cultural life of ancient Greece. Its calendar included an Olympiad-related display, marking the four-year cycle associated with the ancient Greek athletic competitions. This is particularly interesting because it suggests that the device was not limited to observing celestial movements, but brought together astronomy, the measurement of time and the organisation of important cultural events. The same instrument that could calculate lunar cycles and predict eclipses could also help place human activities within a wider understanding of time.There is also evidence that the mechanism may have displayed the positions of planets, although much of the part of its construction has not survived. In a 2018 review published in Nature Astronomy, researchers John H. Seiradakis and Mike Edmunds examined the accumulated findings and discussed how the inscriptions on the surviving fragments support the possibility of planetary displays. The researchers also highlighted the uncertainties that continue to surround its origins, construction and intended purpose.Why the calculator has more questions to answerDespite the extraordinary amount of research carried out on the Antikythera Mechanism, several questions remain unanswered. Its exact maker is unknown, as is the identity of the person or group for whom it was constructed. The shipwreck itself is generally dated to the first century BC, while the mechanism is believed to have been manufactured earlier, around the second century BC. How such an intricate scientific instrument came to be part of the vessel's cargo, and where it was originally intended to travel, remains uncertain. Its discovery also raises questions about how much of ancient mechanical knowledge has been lost, particularly since no surviving device of comparable complexity appears in the historical record for many centuries afterwards.Today, the Antikythera Mechanism stands as one of the most extraordinary surviving examples of ancient Greek scientific ingenuity. Its fragments may be incomplete, its original purpose may never be fully established, who created it may never be known, but the calculations preserved within its corroded gears continue to reveal an entire civilisation that was keenly looking up at the skies with remarkable, unmoving precision.
